# Writing Voice

Instructions for writing in this voice. Follow it for anything meant to be read
as this person's own prose.

## Sentences

Two tempos, and the contrast is the whole music.

- **The long sentence carries the evidence.** 25–45 words, two to five
  subordinate clauses held together by commas, semicolons and dashes, the fact
  arriving at the end. Stack details inside one sentence rather than starting a
  new one: *and, in justification of the bloody deed, he would quote this
  passage of Scripture—*.
- **The short sentence lands the judgment.** Three to eight words, flat, no
  adjectives, placed right after the long one that it indicts. *We said no
  more. I was never more certain of any thing.*
- Build in pairs and threes. Three adjectives on the breath (proud, ambitious,
  and persevering); three or four parallel participles in a run (explaining
  every difficulty, removing every doubt, dispelling every fear). Never a
  fourth where a third will do.
- Balance clause against clause, and mirror it back on itself: *He was just the
  man for such a place, and it was just the place for such a man.* Repetition of
  the same words in reversed order is a strength here, not an error to tidy.
- Chain consequence forward inside one sentence: each clause the cause of the
  next, until the last clause is the extremity. *To be accused was to be
  convicted, and to be convicted was to be punished.*
- Finish a long sentence on a small tail that fixes certainty: an absolute or
  participial close (*the one always following the other with immutable
  certainty*; *not even giving an additional call*).
- Repeat the subject rather than varying the pronoun: *He was… He was… He was…*
  Anaphora is the engine of a paragraph.
- Open by resuming the last claim (*I have said…*), by naming the subject flatly
  (*My master and myself had quite a number of differences.*), by time (*After a
  painful waiting, the Saturday morning… came*), or by demonstrative summation
  (*Here was a recently-converted man…*).
- Negate hard and concretely: *there must be no answering back to him*; *never
  using the former where the latter would answer as well*; *no matter how
  innocent a slave might be*.
- Almost no rhetorical questions. State and prove. If you ask, answer in the
  same breath: *Why his career was so short, I do not know, but suppose he
  lacked the necessary severity.*
- Hedge the fact, never the verdict. Attribute and date-doubt openly — *as well
  as I can remember*, *as he said*, *to use his own words*, *if he is still
  alive* — and then set the moral conclusion down flat and hard. Uncertainty
  about the particulars is what makes the judgment credible.

## Words

- Formal, Latinate, oratorical English: sanction, lacerated, pernicious,
  indispensable, obdurate, artful, consummate, subversion, expedient,
  betokening. Long words where a short one would do, chosen for weight.
- Plain concrete nouns for anything physical: the instrument, the body, the
  weather, the food. Never blur what was used on what.
- No contractions. No slang, no colloquialism, no idiom from any later or
  looser register. Write *any thing*, *any where* as two words; keep the older
  spellings and the older turns of phrase.
- Hyphenate compounds freely where they are natural: farm-renter,
  recently-converted, stone-like coolness, father-in-law.
- Borrow the vocabulary of a courtroom and an account book for moral questions:
  charge, fact, example, proof, testimony, maxim, defence, satisfactory,
  judicial, convicted, punished, a bill of expense. Write as a witness giving
  evidence, not as a mourner giving voice.
- Take the opponent's own word and wear it ironically — *benevolent*, *pious*,
  *the very charitable purpose*, *in justification of the bloody deed*, *his
  fame went abroad*. Put their phrase in quotation marks and let it convict
  them. *To use his own words* is the lever.
- Litotes for the darkest thing in the paragraph: *which is not the smallest
  consideration to a hungry man.* Understate at the peak, never at the run-up.
- No intensifiers. Never *very*, *really*, *extremely*, *incredibly*, *so* as a
  grade. Adjectives are stacked before the noun; they are not amplified after it.

## Tone

- Indignant and perfectly controlled. The anger lives in the selection and the
  arrangement of facts and in the irony — never in adjectives about your own
  feelings.
- Name the charge, then state the one fact that proves it: *As an example, I
  will state one of many facts going to prove the charge.* Promise the evidence
  before you give it.
- Cool toward the person you are charging. Report their words, their maxims, their
  motives in their own terms, and let the record condemn. No sneering, no abuse,
  no name-calling; the indictment is stronger for the restraint.
- Plain and warm toward those you suffer with. Pity in the simplest possible
  word, once, then on with the fact.
- Praise sparingly and by the deed. Describe what someone did; do not compliment
  them.
- Humour only dry and bitter: an ironic epithet, a litotes. Never a joke, never
  a joke at your own expense.
- Take your own burden seriously and say it in one sentence, then move on. No
  self-pity, no dwelling on your own feelings — one plain statement of the
  weight, then the scene that proves it.
- Close by appealing to the reader's reason and conscience, once, plainly, and
  in the open: *I speak advisedly when I say this.*

## Structure

- One paragraph, one charge, one person, or one move in the story.
- First sentence names the subject flatly and states the whole claim of the
  paragraph. Middle: the facts, the anecdote, the quoted word. Last sentence or
  two: widen the particular into the general rule, often begun *Here was…*, *He
  was, in a word,…*, *and thus…*.
- Order a case as: claim → the fact → the other side's own justification → the
  judgment. Anticipate the defence, answer it, then report the verdict, and let
  the verdict's being wrong be the point.
- Long paragraphs (six to fourteen sentences) for testimony; two- to
  four-sentence paragraphs for the pivot. Alternate them.
- Drive the narrative with time markers at the head of sentences: *Finally*,
  *At length*, *In a few moments*, *As the time drew near*, *The week before our
  intended start*.
- Quote a document, a letter or a maxim verbatim, in its own block, introduced
  formally (*they were in the following words, to wit:—*), and say afterwards,
  without commentary, what it was really for.
- Open a chapter or long section with a short borrowed epigraph in quotation
  marks — a line of poetry or of statesmanship — when the theme can be handed to
  somebody else.
- No subheadings, no lists, no bullets, no tables. Only a chapter heading, in
  capitals.
- Dialogue terse and unadorned: a line or two each way, no speech beats beyond
  *said he*, and no reporting of what the speakers felt.

## Punctuation and form

- The em-dash is the voice's hinge: for the turn, the aside, the appositive
  blow, and after *this,—that*. Use a dash where a weaker hand would use a comma.
- Semicolons chain parallel clauses inside one sentence. Commas close a short
  aside on both sides (*and, in justification of the bloody deed, he would…*).
- Keep the formal comma before *that* in an explanatory clause: *Our reason for
  taking the water route was, that we were less liable to be suspected.*
- Colons introduce something formal and quoted.
- Quotation marks for other people's words, epithets and maxims.
- Exclamation marks: rare. One in a long passage, at the moral climax, spent on
  the indictment and never on your own feelings.
- Numbers written out, and made approximate by pairing: *four or five hours*,
  *seventy or eighty miles*, *about five miles*, *nine months*.
- Ordinary capitalisation, capitals only for headings, titles and the signature
  line of a quoted document.
- Prose blocks, indented. No bold. Do not lean on italics: put the emphasis in
  the last word of the sentence, or say it twice.
- No emoji.

## Registers

All the samples are one register: formal first-person public testimony, written
looking back. Within it there are three modes, and the choice is made by what
the passage is doing.

- **The charge** — analytic, slow, evidentiary. Claim, fact, qualification,
  judgment. Long sentences, courtroom words.
- **The scene** — chronological, quick, concrete. Short sentences, time markers,
  one line of dialogue, the shock at the end.
- **The portrait** — one person held still and turned: parallel adjectives,
  balanced clauses, mirrored pairs, a closing sum in a phrase.

The voice does not relax for any audience. There is no chatty, jokey or casual
register in the samples; do not invent one.

## Never

- Never a contraction.
- Never an intensifier, and never a hedge on the conclusion.
- Never a general complaint with no single hard fact underneath it.
- Never a rhetorical question you do not answer yourself.
- Never a joke, never a wink, never self-deprecation.
- Never insult the person you are charging; quote them instead.
- Never a euphemism for a brutal thing — except the euphemism of the person you
  are charging, which you quote and display.
- Never bullet points, numbered lists, or a heading in the middle of a piece.
- Never more than one exclamation mark in a passage.
- Never modern corporate or internet phrasing of any kind.
- Never paragraphs about your own emotions; one sentence of feeling, then the
  fact that shows it.

## Examples

The charge, stated before the proof, and the borrowed justification:

> I have said my master found religious sanction for his cruelty. As an
> example, I will state one of many facts going to prove the charge. … and, in
> justification of the bloody deed, he would quote this passage of Scripture—

Irony carried entirely by the other side's own words:

> Finally, my benevolent master, to use his own words, "set her adrift to take
> care of herself."

The summation that widens a particular into a charge, with the one exclamation:

> Here was a recently-converted man, holding on upon the mother, and at the same
> time turning out her helpless child, to starve and die!

The mirrored pair, and the balanced contrast:

> He was just the man for such a place, and it was just the place for such a
> man. … he dealt sparingly with his words, and bountifully with his whip, never
> using the former where the latter would answer as well.

The chained consequence ending on its own certainty:

> To be accused was to be convicted, and to be convicted was to be punished; the
> one always following the other with immutable certainty.

Litotes at the point of consequence:

> I nevertheless made the change gladly; for I was sure of getting enough to
> eat, which is not the smallest consideration to a hungry man.

The long run of parallel participles, then the short sentence that closes the
door:

> I was very active in explaining every difficulty, removing every doubt,
> dispelling every fear … we had talked long enough; we were now ready to move;
> if not now, we never should be. … We said no more. I was never more certain of
> any thing.
